opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction between engineering and research is a lot blurrier than people expect, especially in frontier AI work. When I talk to people trying to get into safety, they often have this picture where the researchers are the ones having the big ideas and the engineers are implementing them. In practice, a huge amount of progress comes from people who can actually build things well. You have an idea, but testing it means training models, running large experiments, debugging distributed systems, and figuring out why your loss curve looks weird. Being able to do that quickly and reliably is often the bottleneck.

So my general advice is that if you're a strong software engineer and you care about safety, you probably have more leverage than you think. Many of the most impactful people I've worked with came from engineering backgrounds. They didn't necessarily have PhDs in machine learning. They were just very good at writing code, picked up the ML pretty fast once they were in the environment, and were willing to work on whatever was most important rather than whatever was most glamorous.

On the research side, I think there's real value in having people who can step back and ask whether we're working on the right problems at all, who have good taste about which experiments are informative and can design them. That's a real skill, and it's not the same as engineering. But even there, the researchers who are most effective tend to be the ones who are close to the code, who run their own experiments, and who have good intuitions from actually seeing how models behave.

As for how people should choose, I'd encourage them to think less about the title and more about what they're good at and what they enjoy doing day to day. If you love building systems and making things fast and reliable, there's enormous demand for that in safety-relevant work. If you're the kind of person who keeps getting nerd-sniped by conceptual questions about how these systems work, maybe lean toward research. Either way, try to get close to actual models as early as you can. Hands-on experience is extremely valuable, and the field moves quickly enough that you learn a lot just by doing the work.

r002.rationale: It does not compare software engineering practices in PhD-style research with work on a long-lived codebase.

r003.rationale: It does not say that 80,000 Hours steers aspiring safety workers more toward PhD-trained research than software engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that the distinction between "engineering" and "research" is a lot blurrier in practice than people expect from the outside. When I talk to people who are trying to figure out which path to go down, they often have this picture where researchers sit around having ideas and engineers implement them. And that's really not how it works, at least not at the places I've worked. Most of what I do day to day looks like engineering. I'm writing code, I'm debugging distributed systems, I'm trying to figure out why a run went off the rails. The "research" part is mostly about which experiments you choose to run and how you interpret the results, and that's layered on top of a huge amount of engineering work.

So the first piece of advice is: don't undervalue engineering. There's a bit of a status thing where people feel like they need to be doing the "real" research to matter, and I think that's just wrong. The bottleneck at a lot of labs, including on safety teams, is people who can take a vague idea and turn it into a working experiment quickly and reliably. If you can do that, you're enormously useful, and you'll naturally start contributing to the research direction too, because you'll be the one who actually knows what's feasible and what the results look like.

The second thing is that I think people overestimate how much specialized ML background they need before they can contribute. Obviously it helps to understand the basics, how transformers work, how training works, what the common failure modes are. But a strong software engineer who's good at working with large codebases and distributed systems can get up to speed on the ML side surprisingly fast. The reverse is often harder. Someone who knows a lot of theory but hasn't built real systems tends to struggle more, because so much of the work is dealing with the messiness of actually running things at scale.

On the research side, I'd say the thing that matters most is taste, and that's something you mostly develop by doing. Reading papers helps, but what really builds it is running a lot of experiments, being wrong a lot, and slowly getting a sense for which ideas are likely to pan out. So if someone wants to go the research route, my advice is to get into a position where you can run experiments as fast as possible, even if they're small. Replicate results, poke at them, see where they break. That iterative loop is where the learning happens.

And then I'd say, for safety specifically, there's a huge range of work that needs doing. There's interpretability, there's alignment research on how to train models to behave well, there's evaluations, there's the infrastructure that all of that depends on. Some of it is very research-flavored and some of it is almost pure engineering. I'd encourage people to be honest with themselves about what they actually enjoy and are good at, rather than what sounds most impressive, because you're going to be much more effective doing the thing you're motivated to grind on for years.

The last thing I'll say is that I think a lot of people underrate how much you can learn by just applying and seeing what happens. The hiring processes at these places are pretty good at identifying people who can do the work even if their background is unconventional. I've seen people come in from physics, from standard software jobs, from quant finance, and do really well. So I wouldn't spend years trying to build the perfect resume before applying. Build something real, get good at the fundamentals, and then throw your hat in.

astra-6.text:
I think people sometimes picture AI safety as primarily a research career, where you come up with a new idea about how to make a model safe. But there’s a lot of engineering involved in turning an idea into an experiment that tells you something useful. You need to build things, understand why they’re failing, and make sure you’re actually measuring what you think you’re measuring.

So I wouldn’t treat engineering as a fallback if you can’t become a researcher. Someone who can take an ambiguous problem and build a reliable system for investigating it can be incredibly valuable. And the boundary is pretty blurry: an engineer might notice something in an experiment that leads to a research question, while a researcher might spend much of their time writing code.

In terms of choosing a path, I’d look at what you enjoy and where you can get good feedback. Do you like making systems work, debugging, and improving the speed at which a team can run experiments? Or are you more drawn to deciding which questions to ask and interpreting uncertain results? You don’t have to settle that permanently before you start. A role where you work closely with people doing both can help you develop useful skills and figure out where you contribute most.

r001.rationale: The response values engineering in AI safety but does not say experienced software engineers can learn the necessary machine learning relatively quickly.

r002.rationale: It does not compare research training with the software engineering practices needed for a long-lived codebase.

r003.rationale: It does not express an impression that 80,000 Hours steers people more toward PhD research; it only discusses engineering and research career paths generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people sometimes draw too sharp a distinction between engineering and research. A lot of research progress depends on being able to build something, run an experiment, and figure out why the result wasn’t what you expected. So strong engineering skills can give you a lot of leverage on safety research, even if your title isn’t “research scientist.”

The distinction I’d focus on is whether you’re more excited about deciding what questions to ask or about making it possible to answer those questions reliably. Those overlap, but they’re different strengths. You might be very good at building the infrastructure that lets a team run ten times as many useful experiments. Or you might be good at noticing that everyone’s experiments are missing an important question.

If you’re early in your career, I’d look for opportunities where you can get feedback on both. Work on a concrete project with people who can tell you whether your code is good and whether your experiments actually support your conclusions. You don’t need to settle your professional identity before you’ve done that.

And I’d pay a lot of attention to the particular team and project. Having a research title doesn’t automatically mean you’re contributing more to safety. Being an excellent engineer on a team addressing an important safety problem can be an extremely valuable career.
